metadata.title: Tree-based Arithmetic and Compressed Representations of Giant Numbers

nodes.name: Doing arithmetic with a radically different data structure
nodes.statement: Can we do arithmetic in a completely different way, with a radically different data structure? Could this approach provide practical benefits, like operations on giant numbers while having an average performance similar to traditional bitstring representations?
nodes.statement_short: Can arithmetic be redone on a radically different data structure and still handle giant numbers at bitstring-like average speed?

nodes.name: Extra benefits of the tree representation
nodes.statement: While answering these questions positively, our tree based representation described in this paper comes with a few extra benefits: it compresses giant numbers such that, for instance, the largest known prime number as well as its related perfect number are represented as trees of small sizes. The same also applies to Fermat numbers and important computations like exponentiation of two become constant time operations.
nodes.statement_short: The tree representation compresses the largest known prime, perfect and Fermat numbers to small trees and makes exponentiation of 2 constant time.
assumptions: our tree based representation described in this paper
conclusions: it compresses giant numbers such that, for instance, the largest known prime number as well as its related perfect number are represented as trees of small sizes
The same also applies to Fermat numbers and important computations like exponentiation of two become constant time operations.

nodes.name: Succinct representations of sparse sets, multisets and sequences
nodes.statement: At the same time, succinct representations of sparse sets, multisets and sequences become possible through bijections to our tree-represented natural numbers.
assumptions: bijections to our tree-represented natural numbers
conclusions: succinct representations of sparse sets, multisets and sequences become possible

nodes.name: Efficient exotic arithmetic preserving the fundamentals
nodes.statement: With more terrestrial uses in mind, one would simply ask: is it possible to do arithmetic differently, possibly including giant numbers and a radically different underlying data structure, while maintaining the same fundamentals -- addition, multiplication, exponentiation, primality, Peano's axioms behaving in the same way? Moreover, can such exotic arithmetic be as efficient as binary arithmetic, while possibly supporting massively parallel execution?
nodes.statement_short: Can a different underlying data structure keep addition, multiplication, exponentiation, primality and Peano's axioms intact while matching binary arithmetic's efficiency?

nodes.name: Transporting binary recursion equations to tree types
nodes.statement: We have shown in \cite{ppdp10tarau} that type classes and polymorphism can be used to share fundamental operations between natural numbers, finite sequences, sets and multisets. As a consequence of this line of research, we have discovered that it is possible to transport the recursion equations describing binary number arithmetics on natural numbers to various tree types.
nodes.statement_short: Prior work shows type classes let one share arithmetic operations across natural numbers, sequences, sets and multisets, and transport binary recursion equations onto tree types.
assumptions: type classes and polymorphism can be used to share fundamental operations between natural numbers, finite sequences, sets and multisets
conclusions: it is possible to transport the recursion equations describing binary number arithmetics on natural numbers to various tree types

nodes.name: Recursively self-similar run-length encoding of bijective base-2 digits
nodes.statement: However, the representation proposed in this paper is {\em different}. It is arguably simpler, more flexible and likely to support parallel execution of operations. It also allows to easily compute average and worse case complexity bounds. We will describe it in full detail in the next sections, but for the curious reader, it is essentially a {\em recursively self-similar run-length encoding of bijective base-2 digits}.
nodes.statement_short: The paper's representation is essentially a recursively self-similar run-length encoding of bijective base-2 digits.

nodes.name: Literate Haskell executable specification
nodes.statement: To provide a concise view of our compressed tree data type and its operations, we will use the strongly typed functional language Haskell as a precise means to provide an {\em executable} specification. We have adopted a literate programming style, i.e. the code contained in the paper forms a self-contained Haskell module (tested with ghc 7.4.1), also available as a separate file at \url{http://logic.cse.unt.edu/tarau/research/2013/giant.hs} . Also, a Scala package implementing the same tree-based computation is available from \url{http://code.google.com/p/giant-numbers/}. We hope that this will encourage the reader to experiment interactively and validate the technical correctness of our claims.
nodes.statement_short: All code in the paper is a self-contained, executable Haskell module (with a Scala port) so readers can validate the claims.

nodes.name: Haskell notation conventions
nodes.statement: We mention, for the benefit of the reader unfamiliar with Haskell, that a notation like {\tt f x y} stands for $f(x,y)$, {\tt [t]} represents sequences of type {\tt t} and a type declaration like {\tt f :: s -> t -> u} stands for a function $f: s \times t \to u$ (modulo Haskell's ``currying'' operation, given the isomorphism between the function spaces ${s \times t} \to u$ and ${s \to t} \to u$). Our Haskell functions are always represented as sets of recursive equations guided by pattern matching, conditional to constraints (simple arithmetic relations following \verb~|~ and before the \verb~=~ symbol). Locally scoped helper functions are defined in Haskell after the {\tt where} keyword, using the same equational style. The composition of functions {\tt f} and {\tt g} is denoted {\tt f . g}. It is also customary in Haskell, when defining functions in an equational style (using {\tt =}) to write $f=g$ instead of $f~x=g~x$ (``point-free'' notation). The use of Haskell's ``call-by-need'' evaluation allows us to work with infinite sequences, like the {\tt [0..]} infinite list notation, corresponding to the set $\N$ itself.
nodes.statement_short: Notational conventions: curried application, type signatures as functions, guarded recursive equations, where-clauses, function composition, point-free style and lazy infinite lists.

nodes.name: Type classes as approximations of axiom systems
nodes.statement: Haskell's {\em type classes} \cite{DBLP:conf/popl/WadlerB89} are a good approximation of axiom systems as they describe properties and operations generically i.e. in terms of their action on objects of a parametric type. Haskell's type {\em instances} approximate {\em interpretations} \cite{kaye07} of such axiomatizations by providing implementations of the primitive operations, with the added benefit of refining and possibly overriding derived operations with more efficient equivalents.
nodes.statement_short: Type classes play the role of axiom systems and instances the role of interpretations, with the bonus that derived operations may be overridden by faster equivalents.

nodes.name: type class N
nodes.statement: The class {\tt N} assumes only a theory of structural equality (as implemented by the class {\tt Eq} in Haskell). It implements a representation-independent abstraction of natural numbers, allowing us to compare our tree representation with ``ordinary'' natural numbers represented as non-negative arbitrary large {\tt Integers} in Haskell, as well as with a binary representation using bijective base-2 \cite{wiki:bijbase}.
nodes.statement_short: The class {\tt N} is a representation-independent abstraction of natural numbers requiring only structural equality.
differentia: assumes only a theory of structural equality (as implemented by the class {\tt Eq} in Haskell)

nodes.name: The 6 primitive operations of class N
nodes.statement:
e :: n
  o,o',i,i' :: n->n
  o_ :: n->Bool
nodes.definiendum: e, o, o', i, i', o_

nodes.name: Interpretation of the primitive operations
nodes.statement: The constant function {\tt e} can be seen as representing the empty sequence of binary digits. With the usual representation of natural numbers, {\tt e} will be interpreted as {\tt 0}. The constructors {\tt o} and {\tt i} can be seen as applying a function that adds a {\tt 0} or {\tt 1} digit to a binary string on {\tt \{0,1\}$^*$}. The deconstructors {\tt o'} and {\tt i'} undo these operations by removing the corresponding digit. The recognizer {\tt o\_} detects that the constructor {\tt o} is the last one applied, i.e. that the``string ends with the {\tt 0} symbol. It will be interpreted on $\mathbb{N}$ as a recognizer of odd numbers.
nodes.statement_short: {\tt e} is the empty digit sequence (0), {\tt o}/{\tt i} append a 0/1 digit, {\tt o'}/{\tt i'} remove it, and {\tt o\_} recognizes odd numbers.

nodes.name: Derived recognizers e_ and i_
nodes.statement:
e_,i_ :: n->Bool
  e_ x = x == e
  i_ x = not (e_ x || o_ x)
nodes.statement_short: Recognizers for empty and {\tt i}-ending sequences.

nodes.name: Successor s and predecessor s'
nodes.statement:
s,s' :: n->n

  s x | e_ x = o x
  s x | o_ x = i (o' x)
  s x | i_ x = o (s (i' x))

  s' x | x == o e = e
  s' x | i_ x = o (i' x)
  s' x | o_ x = i (s' (o' x))
nodes.statement_short: Successor and predecessor by three guarded equations each, recursing only on the trailing run of equal digits.

nodes.name: bijective base-2 numbers
nodes.statement: By looking at the code, one might notice that our generic definitions of operations mimic recognizers, constructors and destructors for bijective base-2 numbers, i.e. sequences in the language $\{0,1\}^{*}$, similar to binary numbers, except that 0 is represented as the empty sequence and left-delimiting by 1 is omitted.
nodes.statement_short: Bijective base-2 numbers are $\{0,1\}^{*}$ sequences read like binary, but with 0 as the empty sequence and no leading 1 delimiter.
differentia: 0 is represented as the empty sequence

nodes.name: Constant average time of successor and predecessor
nodes.statement: Assuming average constant time for recognizers, constructors and destructors {\tt e\_,o\_o,i\_,i,o',i'}, successor and predecessor {\tt s} and {\tt s'} are constant time, on the average.
nodes.statement_short: If the primitives are constant time on average, then so are {\tt s} and {\tt s'}.
assumptions: Assuming average constant time for recognizers, constructors and destructors {\tt e\_,o\_o,i\_,i,o',i'}
conclusions: successor and predecessor {\tt s} and {\tt s'} are constant time, on the average

nodes.name: Proof of constant average time of s and s'
nodes.statement: Clearly the first two rules are constant time for both {\tt s} and {\tt s'} as they do not make recursive calls. To show that the third rule applies recursion a constant number of times on the average, we observe that the recursion steps are exactly given by the number of 0s or 1s that a (bijective base-2 number) ends with. As only half of them end with a 0 and another half of those end with another 0 etc. one can see that the average number of 0s is bounded by ${1 \over 2}+{1 \over 4}+ \ldots=1$. The same reasoning applies to the average number of 1s a number can end with.
nodes.statement_short: Case analysis on the three guarded rules, bounding the expected trailing-run length by the geometric series ${1 \over 2}+{1 \over 4}+\ldots=1$.

nodes.name: First two rules are non-recursive
nodes.statement: Clearly the first two rules are constant time for both {\tt s} and {\tt s'} as they do not make recursive calls.
nodes.statement_short: Dispose of the two base rules: no recursive calls, hence constant time.

nodes.name: Bounding the recursion depth of the third rule
nodes.statement: To show that the third rule applies recursion a constant number of times on the average, we observe that the recursion steps are exactly given by the number of 0s or 1s that a (bijective base-2 number) ends with. As only half of them end with a 0 and another half of those end with another 0 etc. one can see that the average number of 0s is bounded by ${1 \over 2}+{1 \over 4}+ \ldots=1$.
nodes.statement_short: Identify recursion depth with the trailing run of 0s and bound its average by a geometric series summing to 1.

nodes.name: Symmetric argument for trailing 1s
nodes.statement: The same reasoning applies to the average number of 1s a number can end with.
nodes.statement_short: Conclude by symmetry for trailing 1s.

nodes.name: allFrom (infinite stream of generic natural numbers)
nodes.statement:
allFrom :: n->[n]
  allFrom x = iterate s x
nodes.statement_short: Infinite stream via iterated {\tt s}.

nodes.name: add and sub
nodes.statement:
add :: n->n->n
  add x y | e_ x = y
  add x y | e_ y = x
  add x y | o_ x && o_ y = i (add (o' x) (o' y))
  add x y | o_ x && i_ y = o (s (add (o' x) (i' y)))
  add x y | i_ x && o_ y = o (s (add (i' x) (o' y)))
  add x y | i_ x && i_ y = i (s (add (i' x) (i' y)))

  sub :: n->n->n
  sub x y | e_ y = x
  sub y x | o_ y && o_ x = s' (o (sub (o' y) (o' x)))
  sub y x | o_ y && i_ x = s' (s' (o (sub (o' y) (i' x))))
  sub y x | i_ y && o_ x = o (sub (i' y) (o' x))
  sub y x | i_ y && i_ x = s' (o (sub (i' y) (i' x)))
nodes.statement_short: Digit-wise recursive addition and subtraction driven by the parity of the two operands' last digits.

nodes.name: Linear complexity of generic addition and subtraction
nodes.statement: It is easy to see that addition and subtraction are implemented generically, with asymptotic complexity proportional to the size of the operands.
assumptions: addition and subtraction are implemented generically
conclusions: asymptotic complexity proportional to the size of the operands

nodes.name: cmp (comparison)
nodes.statement:
cmp :: n->n->Ordering
  cmp x y | e_ x && e_ y = EQ
  cmp x _ | e_ x = LT
  cmp _ y | e_ y = GT
  cmp x y | o_ x && o_ y = cmp (o' x) (o' y)
  cmp x y | i_ x && i_ y = cmp (i' x) (i' y)
  cmp x y | o_ x && i_ y = down (cmp (o' x) (i' y)) where
    down EQ = LT
    down r = r
  cmp x y | i_ x && o_ y = up (cmp (i' x) (o' y)) where
    up EQ = GT
    up r = r
nodes.statement_short: Recursive three-way comparison that strips matching digits and breaks ties by which operand ends in {\tt o} versus {\tt i}.

nodes.name: cmp induces the expected total order on N
nodes.statement: Comparison provides the expected total order of $\N$ on our type class:
assumptions: our type class
conclusions: Comparison provides the expected total order of $\N$

nodes.name: min2 and max2
nodes.statement:
min2,max2 :: n->n->n
  min2 x y = if LT==cmp x y then x else y
  max2 x y = if LT==cmp x y then y else x
nodes.statement_short: Minimum and maximum of two numbers, selected by a single {\tt cmp} test.

nodes.name: mul (multiplication)
nodes.statement:
mul :: n->n->n
  mul x _ | e_ x = e
  mul _ y | e_ y = e
  mul x y = s (m (s' x) (s' y)) where
    m x y | e_ x = y
    m x y | o_ x = o (m (o' x) y)
    m x y | i_ x = s (add y (o (m (i' x) y)))
nodes.statement_short: Shift-and-add multiplication on predecessors, with a helper {\tt m} recursing on the digits of the first operand.

nodes.name: db (double) and hf (half)
nodes.statement:
db,hf :: n->n 
  db = s' . o
  hf = s . i'
nodes.statement_short: Double and half of a number.

nodes.name: pow (power)
nodes.statement:
pow :: n->n->n
  pow _ y | e_ y = o e
  pow x y | o_ y = mul x (pow (mul x x) (o' y))
  pow x y | i_ y = mul (mul x x) (pow (mul x x) (i' y))
nodes.statement_short: Binary (repeated-squaring) exponentiation driven by the digits of the exponent.

nodes.name: exp2 and leftshift
nodes.statement:
exp2 :: n->n
  exp2 x | e_ x = o e
  exp2 x = db (exp2 (s' x)) 

  leftshift :: n->n->n
  leftshift x y = mul (exp2 x) y
nodes.statement_short: Generic exponent of 2 by repeated doubling, and left shift as multiplication by a power of 2.

nodes.name: div_and_rem, divide and reminder
nodes.statement:
div_and_rem :: n->n->(n,n)

  div_and_rem x y | LT == cmp x y = (e,x)
  div_and_rem x y | not (e_ y) = (q,r) where 
    (qt,rm) = divstep x y
    (z,r) = div_and_rem rm y
    q = add (exp2 qt) z

    divstep :: N n => n->n->(n,n)
    divstep n m = (q, sub n p) where
      q = try_to_double n m e
      p = mul (exp2 q) m

      try_to_double x y k = 
        if (LT==cmp x y) 
          then s' k
          else try_to_double x (db y) (s k)

  divide,reminder :: n->n->n

  divide n m = fst (div_and_rem n m)
  reminder n m = snd (div_and_rem n m)
nodes.statement_short: Division by repeated doubling of the divisor to find the largest fitting power of 2, then recursing on the remainder.

nodes.name: instance N Integer
nodes.statement:
instance N Integer where
  e = 0

  o_ x = odd x

  o  x = 2*x+1
  o' x | odd x && x >  0 = (x-1) `div` 2

  i  x = 2*x+2
  i' x | even x && x > 0 = (x-2) `div` 2
nodes.statement_short: Interpretation of the primitives over Haskell's arbitrary-length {\tt Integer}: {\tt o x = 2*x+1}, {\tt i x = 2*x+2}.
nodes.genus: an instance built around the (arbitrary length) {\tt Integer} type
differentia: also usable as a witness on the time/space complexity of our operations

nodes.name: datatype B and instance N B
nodes.statement:
data B = B | O B | I B deriving (Show, Read, Eq)

instance N B where
  e = B
  o = O
  i = I

  o' (O x) = x
  i' (I x) = x

  o_ (O _) = True
  o_ _ = False
nodes.statement_short: The bijective base-2 datatype {\tt B} with constructors {\tt O}/{\tt I}, whose {\tt N} instance maps the abstract primitives to actual constructors.
nodes.genus: An instance mapping our abstract operations to actual constructors
differentia: data B = B | O B | I B

nodes.name: Trying out operations on the Integer and B instances
nodes.statement:
*Giant> mul 10 5
50
*Giant> exp2 5
32
*Giant> add (O B) (I (O B))
O (I B)

nodes.name: datatype T (tree represented natural numbers)
nodes.statement: data T = T | V T [T] | W T [T] deriving (Eq,Show,Read)
nodes.statement_short: Run-length counter trees for naturals.
nodes.section: 4 Computing with our compressed tree representations
nodes.definiendum: the data type for our tree represented natural numbers
differentia: The type {\tt T} corresponds to an empty sequence
the type {\tt V x xs} counts the number {\tt x} of {\tt o} applications followed by an alternation of similar counts of {\tt i} and {\tt o} applications
the type {\tt W x xs} counts the number {\tt x} of {\tt i} applications followed by an alternation of similar counts of {\tt o} and {\tt i} applications
the same principle is applied recursively for the counters, until the empty sequence is reached

nodes.name: Intuition behind the union type T
nodes.statement: The intuition behind this ``union type'' is the following: \begin{itemize} \item The type {\tt T} corresponds to an empty sequence \item the type {\tt V x xs} counts the number {\tt x} of {\tt o} applications followed by an alternation of similar counts of {\tt i} and {\tt o} applications \item the type {\tt W x xs} counts the number {\tt x} of {\tt i} applications followed by an alternation of similar counts of {\tt o} and {\tt i} applications \item the same principle is applied recursively for the counters, until the empty sequence is reached \end{itemize} One can see this process as run-length compressed bijective base-2 numbers, represented as trees with either empty leaves or at least one branch, after applying the encoding recursively.
nodes.statement_short: {\tt V}/{\tt W} nodes record run lengths of {\tt o}/{\tt i} applications, recursively encoded, i.e. run-length compressed bijective base-2 numbers as trees.
nodes.section: 4 Computing with our compressed tree representations

nodes.name: instance N T (the 6 primitive operations on trees)
nodes.statement:
instance N T where
  e = T

  o T = V T []
  o (V x xs) = V (s x) xs
  o (W x xs) = V T (x:xs)

  i T = W T []
  i (V x xs) = W T (x:xs)
  i (W x xs) = W (s x) xs

  o' (V T []) = T
  o' (V T (x:xs)) = W x xs
  o' (V x xs) = V (s' x) xs

  i' (W T []) = T
  i' (W T (x:xs)) = V x xs
  i' (W x xs) = W (s' x) xs

  o_ (V _ _ ) = True
  o_ _ = False
nodes.statement_short: The six primitives on trees: {\tt o}/{\tt i} increment or open a run counter, {\tt o'}/{\tt i'} decrement or close it, {\tt o\_} tests for a {\tt V} node.
nodes.section: 4 Computing with our compressed tree representations

nodes.name: exp2' and leftshift' (overrides for type T)
nodes.statement:
exp2 = exp2' where
    exp2' T = V T []
    exp2' x = s (V (s' x) [])

  leftshift = leftshift' where
    leftshift' _ T = T
    leftshift' n y | o_ y = s (vmul n (s' y))
    leftshift' n y | i_ y = s (vmul (s n) (s' y))
nodes.statement_short: Constant-time-on-average exponent of 2 and left shift for trees, built directly from a {\tt V} node and {\tt vmul}.
nodes.section: 4 Computing with our compressed tree representations

nodes.name: vmul
nodes.statement:
vmul T y = y
vmul n T = V (s' n) []
vmul n (V y ys) = V (add (s' n) y) ys
vmul n (W y ys) = V (s' n) (y:ys)
nodes.statement_short: Constant-time repeated {\tt o} application via the head run counter.
nodes.section: 4 Computing with our compressed tree representations

nodes.name: Number-theoretic basis of the exp2' and leftshift' overridings
nodes.statement: Note that such overridings take advantage of the specific encoding, as a result of simple number theoretic observations. For instance, the operation {\tt exp2'} works in time proportional to {\tt s} and {\tt s'}, that can be shown to be constant on the average. The more complex {\tt leftshift'} operation observes that repeated application of the {\tt o} operation, when adjusted based on being even or odd, provides an efficient implementation of multiplication with an exponent of 2.
nodes.statement_short: {\tt exp2'} costs only an {\tt s}/{\tt s'} (constant on average) and {\tt leftshift'} turns repeated {\tt o} application into multiplication by a power of 2.
nodes.section: 4 Computing with our compressed tree representations
assumptions: such overridings take advantage of the specific encoding, as a result of simple number theoretic observations
conclusions: the operation {\tt exp2'} works in time proportional to {\tt s} and {\tt s'}, that can be shown to be constant on the average
repeated application of the {\tt o} operation, when adjusted based on being even or odd, provides an efficient implementation of multiplication with an exponent of 2

nodes.name: view (polymorphic converter between instances of N)
nodes.statement:
view :: (N a,N b)=>a->b
view x | e_ x = e
view x | o_ x = o (view (o' x))
view x | i_ x = i (view (i' x))
nodes.statement_short: Convert between any two {\tt N} instances by structural recursion.
nodes.section: 4 Computing with our compressed tree representations

nodes.name: t, b and n (specializations of view)
nodes.statement:
t :: (N n) => n -> T
t = view

b :: (N n) => n -> B
b = view

n :: (N n) => n -> Integer
n = view
nodes.statement_short: Specializations of {\tt view} to trees, base-2 and {\tt Integer}.
nodes.section: 4 Computing with our compressed tree representations

nodes.name: Converting 42 between the three representations
nodes.statement:
*Giant> t 42
W (V T []) [T,T,T]
*Giant> b it
I (I (O (I (O B))))
*Giant> n it
42

nodes.name: Correctness proofs omitted for space
nodes.statement: While space constraints forbid us from providing the correctness proofs of operations like {\tt exp2'} and {\tt leftshift'}, we are able to illustrate their expected usage as follows:
nodes.section: 4 Computing with our compressed tree representations

nodes.name: Expected usage of exp2 and leftshift on trees
nodes.statement:
*Giant> t 5
V T [T]
*Giant> exp2 it
W T [V (V T []) []]
*Giant> n it
32
*Giant> t 10
W (V T []) [T]
*Giant> leftshift it (t 1)
W T [W T [V T []]]
*Giant> n it
1024

nodes.name: Compact tree expressions of Fermat, Mersenne and perfect numbers
nodes.statement: Let's first observe that Fermat, Mersenne and perfect numbers have all compact expressions with our tree representation of type {\tt T}.
nodes.section: 5 Efficient representation of some important number-theoretical entities
assumptions: our tree representation of type {\tt T}
conclusions: Fermat, Mersenne and perfect numbers have all compact expressions

nodes.name: fermat, mersenne and perfect numbers
nodes.statement:
fermat n = s (exp2 (exp2 n))

mersenne p = s' (exp2 p)

perfect p = s (V q [q]) where q = s' (s' p)
nodes.statement_short: Fermat $2^{2^n}+1$, Mersenne $2^p-1$ and perfect numbers as trees.

nodes.name: Space-efficient T representations of sparse collections
nodes.statement: We will now describe bijective mappings between collection types as well as a G\"odel numbering scheme putting them in bijection with natural numbers. Interestingly, natural number encodings for sparse instances of these collections will have space-efficient representations as natural numbers of type {\tt T}, in contrast with bitstring or conventional {\tt Integer}-based representations.
nodes.statement_short: G\"odel-numbered sparse sets, multisets and lists are space-efficient as type {\tt T} naturals, unlike bitstring or {\tt Integer} encodings.
nodes.section: 6 Representing sparse sets, multisets and lists
assumptions: natural number encodings for sparse instances of these collections
conclusions: space-efficient representations as natural numbers of type {\tt T}, in contrast with bitstring or conventional {\tt Integer}-based representations

nodes.name: the bijection $f(x,y)=2^{x}(2y+1)$
nodes.statement: The type class {\tt Collections} will convert between natural numbers and lists, by using the bijection $f(x,y)=2^{x}(2y+1)$, implemented by the function {\tt c} and its first and second projections {\tt c'} and {\tt c''}, inverting it.
nodes.statement_short: Pairing bijection $f(x,y)=2^{x}(2y+1)$ with projections {\tt c'} and {\tt c''}.
nodes.section: 6 Representing sparse sets, multisets and lists

nodes.name: type class Collections
nodes.statement:
class (N n) => Collections n where
  c :: n->n->n
  c',c'' :: n->n

  c x y = mul (exp2 x) (o y)

  c' x | not (e_ x) = if o_ x then e else s (c' (hf x))
  c'' x | not (e_ x) = if o_ x then o' x else c'' (hf x)
nodes.statement_short: Class extending {\tt N} with the pairing function {\tt c x y = mul (exp2 x) (o y)} and its two projections.
nodes.section: 6 Representing sparse sets, multisets and lists
differentia: convert between natural numbers and lists, by using the bijection $f(x,y)=2^{x}(2y+1)$

nodes.name: to_list and from_list
nodes.statement:
to_list :: n->[n]
  to_list x | e_ x = []
  to_list x = (c' x) : (to_list (c'' x))

  from_list:: [n]->n
  from_list [] = e
  from_list (x:xs) = c x (from_list xs)
nodes.statement_short: Bijection between naturals and lists of naturals by repeatedly applying the pairing projections {\tt c'}/{\tt c''} and, inversely, {\tt c}.
nodes.section: 6 Representing sparse sets, multisets and lists

nodes.name: Incremental sums transform lists to multisets and sets
nodes.statement: Incremental sums are used to transform arbitrary lists to multisets and sets, inverted by pairwise differences.
nodes.section: 6 Representing sparse sets, multisets and lists

nodes.name: list2mset, mset2list, list2set and set2list
nodes.statement:
list2mset, mset2list, list2set, set2list :: [n]->[n]

  list2mset ns = tail (scanl add e ns)
  mset2list ms = zipWith sub ms (e:ms)

  list2set = (map s') . list2mset . (map s)
  set2list = (map s') . mset2list . (map s)
nodes.statement_short: Prefix sums map lists to multisets (pairwise differences invert it), and the same shifted by {\tt s}/{\tt s'} gives strictly increasing sets.
nodes.section: 6 Representing sparse sets, multisets and lists

nodes.name: to_mset, from_mset, to_set and from_set
nodes.statement:
to_mset, to_set :: n->[n]
  from_mset, from_set :: [n]->n

  to_mset = list2mset . to_list
  from_mset = from_list . mset2list

  to_set = list2set . to_list
  from_set = from_list . set2list
nodes.statement_short: Compose the natural-number-to-list bijection with the list-to-multiset/set transforms to obtain bijections to multisets and sets.
nodes.section: 6 Representing sparse sets, multisets and lists

nodes.name: vmul shortcut speeds up the list-to-natural-number bijection
nodes.statement: A simple number-theoretic observation connecting $2^{n}$ and $n$ applications of the constructor {\tt i}, implemented by the function {\tt vmul}, allows a shortcut that speeds up the bijection from lists to natural numbers, by overriding the functions {\tt c, c', c''} in instance {\tt T}.
nodes.statement_short: Relating $2^{n}$ to $n$ applications of {\tt i} lets {\tt c, c', c''} be overridden in instance {\tt T} for a faster list-to-number bijection.
nodes.section: 6 Representing sparse sets, multisets and lists
assumptions: A simple number-theoretic observation connecting $2^{n}$ and $n$ applications of the constructor {\tt i}, implemented by the function {\tt vmul}
conclusions: allows a shortcut that speeds up the bijection from lists to natural numbers, by overriding the functions {\tt c, c', c''} in instance {\tt T}

nodes.name: instance Collections T (cons, hd, tl)
nodes.statement:
instance Collections B
instance Collections Integer
instance Collections T where
  c = cons where
    cons n y = s (vmul n (s' (o y)))

  c' = hd where  
    hd z | o_ z = T
    hd z = s x where
      V x _ = s' z

  c'' = tl where
    tl z | o_ z = o' z 
    tl z = f xs where
      V _ xs = s' z

      f [] = T
      f (y:ys) = s (i' (W y ys))
nodes.statement_short: Tree-specialized pairing: {\tt c} via {\tt vmul}, and projections that read the head counter and the tail list of a {\tt V} node directly.

nodes.name: Trees of type T give a more compact representation of sparse sets
nodes.statement: As the following example shows, trees of type {\tt T} offer a significantly more compact representation of sparse sets.
nodes.section: 6 Representing sparse sets, multisets and lists
conclusions: trees of type {\tt T} offer a significantly more compact representation of sparse sets

nodes.name: Dense sets compress as duals of sparse ones
nodes.statement: Note that a similar compression occurs for sets of natural numbers with only a few elements missing, as they have the same representation size with type {\tt T} as the {\tt dual} of their sparse counterpart.
nodes.statement_short: Almost-full sets compress as well as sparse ones, being {\tt dual}s of them.

nodes.name: Bitwise operations borrowed from ordered set operations
nodes.statement: As an application, we can define bitwise operations on our natural numbers by borrowing the corresponding ordered set operations, provided in Haskell by the package {\tt Data.List.Ordered}.
nodes.section: 6 Representing sparse sets, multisets and lists

nodes.name: type class BitwiseOperations and l_op
nodes.statement:
class Collections n => BitwiseOperations n where 
  l_op :: ([n]->[n]->[n])->n->n->n
  l_op op x y = from_set (op (to_set x) (to_set y))
nodes.statement_short: Higher-order transport of a binary ordered-set operation to natural numbers via {\tt to\_set}/{\tt from\_set}.
nodes.section: 6 Representing sparse sets, multisets and lists
nodes.definiendum: the type class {\tt BitwiseOperations} and the higher order function {\tt l\_op}
differentia: transporting a binary operation from ordered sets to natural numbers

nodes.name: l_and, l_or, l_xor and l_dif
nodes.statement:
l_and,l_or,l_xor,l_dif:: n->n->n
  l_and = l_op (isectBy cmp)
  l_or = l_op (unionBy cmp)
  l_xor = l_op (xunionBy cmp)
  l_dif = l_op (minusBy cmp)
nodes.statement_short: Bitwise and/or/xor/difference obtained by transporting ordered-set intersection, union, symmetric difference and difference.
nodes.section: 6 Representing sparse sets, multisets and lists

nodes.name: l_ite (bitwise if-then-else)
nodes.statement:
l_ite :: n->n->n->n
  l_ite x y z = from_set (ite (to_set x) (to_set y) (to_set z)) where
    ite d a b =  xunionBy cmp e b where
      c = xunionBy cmp a b
      e = isectBy cmp c d
nodes.statement_short: Ternary bitwise if-then-else composed from symmetric differences and an intersection on ordered sets.
nodes.section: 6 Representing sparse sets, multisets and lists

nodes.name: l_not (bitwise negation)
nodes.statement:
l_not :: Integer->n->n
  l_not l x |xl<=l = from_set (minusBy cmp ms xs) where
    xs = to_set x
    xl = genericLength xs
    ms = genericTake l (allFrom e)
nodes.statement_short: Bitwise negation as set complement with respect to $2^{l}-1$, i.e. the set of all elements up to {\tt l}.
nodes.section: 6 Representing sparse sets, multisets and lists

nodes.name: Generalizing the iso-functor mechanism
nodes.statement: We will next generalize the iso-functor mechanism implemented generically by {\tt l\_op} that transports operations back an forth between data types as a special data type, consisting of two higher order functions inverse to each other.
nodes.section: 6 Representing sparse sets, multisets and lists

nodes.name: Iso data type
nodes.statement:
data Iso a b = Iso (a->b) (b->a)

from (Iso f _) = f
to (Iso _ f') = f'
nodes.statement_short: An isomorphism as a pair of inverse functions.
differentia: consisting of two higher order functions inverse to each other

nodes.name: as, lend1 and lend2
nodes.statement:
as that this x = to that (from this x)

lend1 op1 (Iso f f') x = f' (op1 (f x))
lend2 op2 (Iso f f') x y = f' (op2 (f x) (f y))
nodes.statement_short: Morph a value between two virtual types, and lend a unary or binary operation across an isomorphism.

nodes.name: virtual types nat, list, mset and set
nodes.statement:
nat = Iso id id
list = Iso from_list to_list
mset = Iso from_mset to_mset
set = Iso from_set to_set
nodes.statement_short: Virtual types nat, list, mset, set as isomorphisms.
nodes.genus: ``virtual types'' centered around type class {\tt N}

nodes.name: A small embedded language morphing between data types
nodes.statement: This results in a small ``embedded language'' that morphs between various instances of type class {\tt N} and their corresponding list, multiset and set types, as follows:

nodes.name: Morphing 1234 between nat, set and tree types
nodes.statement:
*Giant> as set nat 1234
[1,4,6,7,10]
*Giant> map t it
[V T [],W T [T],W (V T []) [],V (W T []) [],W (V T []) [T]]
*Giant> as nat set it
W (V T []) [V T [],T,T,V T [],V T []]
*Giant> n it
1234
*Giant> lend1 s set [0,2,3]
[1,2,3]
*Giant> lend2 add set [0,2,3] [4,5]
[0,2,3,4,5]

nodes.name: The type class SpecialComputations
nodes.statement: A number of other, somewhat more common computations also benefit from our data representations. The type class {\tt SpecialComputations} groups them together and provides their bitstring inspired generic implementations.

nodes.name: dual
nodes.statement:
class Collections n => SpecialComputations n where
  dual :: n->n
  dual x | e_ x = e
  dual x | o_ x = i (dual (o' x))
  dual x | i_ x = o (dual (i' x))
nodes.statement_short: Flip every {\tt o} into an {\tt i} and vice versa, i.e. complement the bijective base-2 digits.

nodes.name: bitsize
nodes.statement:
bitsize :: n->n
  bitsize x | e_ x = e
  bitsize x | o_ x = s (bitsize (o' x))
  bitsize x | i_ x = s (bitsize (i' x))
nodes.statement_short: Count the number of {\tt o} and {\tt i} applications by structural recursion.

nodes.name: repsize
nodes.statement:
-- representation size - defaults to bitsize
  repsize :: n->n
  repsize = bitsize
nodes.statement_short: Representation size, defaulting to the bijective base-2 bitsize.

nodes.name: decons and cons are bijections between N-{0} and N x N
nodes.statement: The functions {\tt decons} and {\tt cons} provide bijections between $\N-\{0\}$ and $\N \times \N$ and can be used as an alternative mechanism for building bijections between lists, multisets and sets of natural numbers and natural numbers. They are based on separating {\tt o} and {\tt i} applications that build up a natural number represented in bijective base 2.
nodes.statement_short: {\tt cons}/{\tt decons} form a bijection $\N-\{0\} \leftrightarrow \N \times \N$ by splitting off the leading run of equal digits.
assumptions: They are based on separating {\tt o} and {\tt i} applications that build up a natural number represented in bijective base 2
conclusions: The functions {\tt decons} and {\tt cons} provide bijections between $\N-\{0\}$ and $\N \times \N$
can be used as an alternative mechanism for building bijections between lists, multisets and sets of natural numbers and natural numbers

nodes.name: decons and cons
nodes.statement:
decons ::n->(n,n)
  cons :: (n,n)->n

  decons z | o_ z = (x,y) where
    x0 = s' (ocount z)
    y = otrim z
    x = if e_ y then (s'.o) x0 else x0 
  decons z | i_ z = (x,y) where
    x0 = s' (icount z)
    y = itrim z
    x = if e_ y then (s'.i) x0 else x0 

  cons (x,y) | e_ x && e_ y = s e
  cons (x,y) | o_ x && e_ y = itimes (s (i' (s x))) e
  cons (x,y) | i_ x && e_ y = otimes (s (o' (s x))) e
  cons (x,y) | o_ y = itimes (s x) y
  cons (x,y) | i_ y = otimes (s x) y
nodes.statement_short: Split a number into (length of its leading digit run, remaining number) and rebuild it by repeated {\tt o}/{\tt i} application.

nodes.name: ocount, icount, otrim and itrim
nodes.statement:
ocount,icount,otrim,itrim :: n->n

  ocount x | o_ x = s (ocount (o' x))
  ocount _ = e

  icount x | i_ x = s (icount (i' x))
  icount _ = e

  otrim x | o_ x = otrim (o' x)
  otrim x = x

  itrim x | i_ x = itrim (i' x)
  itrim x = x
nodes.statement_short: Count and strip the trailing run of {\tt o} (resp. {\tt i}) applications.

nodes.name: otimes and itimes
nodes.statement:
otimes,itimes :: n->n->n

  otimes x y | e_ x = y
  otimes x y = otimes (s' x) (o y)

  itimes x y | e_ x = y
  itimes x y = itimes (s' x) (i y)
nodes.statement_short: Apply the constructor {\tt o} (resp. {\tt i}) exactly {\tt x} times to {\tt y}.

nodes.name: to_list' and from_list'
nodes.statement:
to_list' :: n->[n]
  to_list' x | e_ x = []
  to_list' x = hd : (to_list' tl) where (hd,tl)=decons x

  from_list' :: [n]->n
  from_list' [] = e
  from_list' (x:xs) = cons (x,from_list' xs)
nodes.statement_short: An alternative natural-number/list bijection obtained by iterating {\tt decons} and {\tt cons}.

nodes.name: Asymptotic complexity reduction from tbitsize and tdual
nodes.statement: One can observe the significant reduction of asymptotic complexity with respect to the default operations provided by the type class {\tt SpecialComputations} when overriding with {\tt tbitsize} and {\tt tdual} in instance {\tt T}.
assumptions: when overriding with {\tt tbitsize} and {\tt tdual} in instance {\tt T}
conclusions: significant reduction of asymptotic complexity with respect to the default operations provided by the type class {\tt SpecialComputations}

nodes.name: instance SpecialComputations T (tbitsize, tdual, tsize)
nodes.statement:
instance SpecialComputations Integer
instance SpecialComputations B
instance SpecialComputations T where
  bitsize = tbitsize where
    tbitsize T = T
    tbitsize (V x xs) = s (foldr add1 x xs)
    tbitsize (W x xs) = s (foldr add1 x xs)

    add1 x y = s (add x y)

  dual = tdual where
    tdual T = T
    tdual (V x xs) = W x xs
    tdual (W x xs) = V x xs 

  repsize = tsize where
    tsize T = T
    tsize (V x xs) = s (foldr add T (map tsize (x:xs)))
    tsize (W x xs) = s (foldr add T (map tsize (x:xs)))
nodes.statement_short: Tree overrides: bitsize as a fold of the run counters, dual as a single {\tt V}/{\tt W} swap, and repsize as the recursive node count.

nodes.name: Special purpose cons/decons code is even more significant
nodes.statement: The replacement with special purpose code for the {\tt cons / decons} functions is even more significant:

nodes.name: decons and cons overridden for type T
nodes.statement:
decons (V x []) = ((s'.o) x,T)
  decons (V x (y:ys)) = (x,W y ys)
  decons (W x []) = ((s'.i) x,T)
  decons (W x (y:ys)) = (x,V y ys)

  cons (T,T) = V T []
  cons (x,T) | o_ x =  W (i' (s x)) []
  cons (x,T) | i_ x = V (o' (s x)) []
  cons (x,V y ys) = W x (y:ys)
  cons (x,W y ys) = V x (y:ys)
nodes.statement_short: On trees, {\tt cons}/{\tt decons} become constant-time head/tail manipulations of the {\tt V}/{\tt W} counter list.

nodes.name: cons/decons cost is proportional to s and s' on trees
nodes.statement: One can also see that their complexity is now proportional to {\tt s} and {\tt s'} given that the {\tt V} and {\tt W} operations perform in constant time the work of {\tt otimes} and {\tt itimes}.
assumptions: the {\tt V} and {\tt W} operations perform in constant time the work of {\tt otimes} and {\tt itimes}
conclusions: their complexity is now proportional to {\tt s} and {\tt s'}

nodes.name: Shorter lists close to powers of 2
nodes.statement: Note the shorter lists created close to powers of 2, coming from the longer sequences of consecutive {\tt o} and {\tt i}m operations in that region.

nodes.name: Two objectives of the performance measurements
nodes.statement: Our performance measurements (run on a Mac Air with 8GB of memory and an Intel i7 processor) serve two objectives: \begin{enumerate} \item to show that, on the average, our tree based representations perform on a blend of arithmetic computations within a small constant factor compared with conventional bitstring-based computations \item to show that on interesting special computations they outperform the conventional ones due to the much lower asymptotic complexity of such operations on data type {\tt T}. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Benchmarks aim to show average performance within a small constant factor of bitstrings, and much better performance on special computations.
conclusions: to show that, on the average, our tree based representations perform on a blend of arithmetic computations within a small constant factor compared with conventional bitstring-based computations
to show that on interesting special computations they outperform the conventional ones due to the much lower asymptotic complexity of such operations on data type {\tt T}

nodes.name: Benchmarks serving objective 1
nodes.statement: Objective {\em 1} is served by the Ackerman function that exercises the successor and predecessor functions quite heavily, the prime generation and the Lucas-Lehmer primality test for Mersenne numbers that exercise a blend of arithmetic operations.

nodes.name: Benchmarks serving objective 2
nodes.statement: Objective {\em 2} is served by the other benchmarks that take advantage of the overriding by instance {\tt T} of operations like {\tt exp2} and {\tt bitsize}, as well as the compressed representation of large numbers like the 45-th Mersenne prime and perfect numbers. In some cases the conventional representations are unable to run these benchmarks within existing computer memory and CPU-power limitations (marked with {\tt ?} in the comparison table of Fig. \ref{perf}). In other cases, like in the sparse set encoding benchmark, data type {\tt T} performs significantly faster than binary representations.
nodes.statement_short: The remaining benchmarks exploit the {\tt T} overrides of {\tt exp2}/{\tt bitsize} and compressed giant numbers, where conventional representations sometimes cannot run at all.

nodes.name: Tree representations are competitive and sometimes much faster
nodes.statement: Together they indicate that our tree-based representations are likely to be competitive with existing bitstring-based packages on typical computations and significantly outperform them on some number-theoretically interesting computations. While the code of the benchmarks is omitted due to space constraints, it is part of the companion Haskell file at \url{http://logic.cse.unt.edu/tarau/Research/2013/giant.hs}.
nodes.statement_short: The benchmarks suggest tree representations are competitive in general and far better on number-theoretically interesting computations.
conclusions: our tree-based representations are likely to be competitive with existing bitstring-based packages on typical computations and significantly outperform them on some number-theoretically interesting computations

nodes.name: Knuth's arrow-up notation
nodes.statement: Several notations for very large numbers have been invented in the past. Examples include Knuth's {\em arrow-up} notation \cite{knuthUp} covering operations like the {\em tetration} (a notation for towers of exponents). In contrast to our tree-based natural numbers, such notations are not closed under addition and multiplication, and consequently they cannot be used as a replacement for ordinary binary or decimal numbers.
nodes.statement_short: Arrow-up/tetration notations denote huge numbers but are not closed under addition and multiplication, unlike the tree representation.

nodes.name: Goodstein's theorem
nodes.statement: The first instance of a hereditary number system, at our best knowledge, occurs in the proof of Goodstein's theorem \cite{goodstein}, where replacement of finite numbers on a tree's branches by the ordinal $\omega$ allows him to prove that a ``hailstone sequence'' visiting arbitrarily large numbers eventually turns around and terminates.
nodes.statement_short: Goodstein's theorem: hailstone sequences visiting arbitrarily large numbers eventually terminate, proved via a hereditary number system with the ordinal $\omega$.
assumptions: replacement of finite numbers on a tree's branches by the ordinal $\omega$
conclusions: a ``hailstone sequence'' visiting arbitrarily large numbers eventually turns around and terminates

nodes.name: Numeration systems on regular languages
nodes.statement: Numeration systems on regular languages have been studied recently, e.g. in \cite{Rigo2001469} and specific instances of them are also known as bijective base-k numbers \cite{wiki:bijbase}. Arithmetic packages similar to our bijective base-2 view of arithmetic operations are part of libraries of proof assistants like Coq \cite{Coq:manual} and the corresponding regular languages have been used as a basis of decidable arithmetic systems like {\tt (W)S1S} \cite{buchi62} and {\tt (W)S2S} \cite{Rabin69Decidability}.
nodes.statement_short: Bijective base-k numbers arise as numeration systems on regular languages, also used in Coq's arithmetic libraries and in the decidable systems (W)S1S and (W)S2S.

nodes.name: Arithmetic on the free magma of binary trees
nodes.statement: Arithmetic computations based on recursive data types like the free magma of binary trees (isomorphic to the context-free language of balanced parentheses) are described in \cite{sac12} and \cite{padl12}, where they are seen as G\"odel's {\tt System T} types, as well as combinator application trees. In \cite{ppdp10tarau} a type class mechanism is used to express computations on hereditarily finite sets and hereditarily finite functions.
nodes.statement_short: Earlier tree-based arithmetic used the free magma of binary trees and type classes over hereditarily finite sets and functions.

nodes.name: Emulation of Peano and binary arithmetic in Prolog
nodes.statement: An emulation of Peano and conventional binary arithmetic operations in Prolog, is described in \cite{DBLP:conf/flops/KiselyovBFS08}. Their approach is similar as far as a symbolic representation is used. The key difference with our work is that our operations work on tree structures, and as such, they are not based on previously known algorithms.
nodes.statement_short: Prolog emulations of Peano/binary arithmetic are also symbolic, but operate on strings rather than on trees.

nodes.name: Arithmetic with C++ templates and Haskell type inference
nodes.statement: Arithmetic computations with types expressed as {\tt C++} templates are described in \cite{DBLP:journals/corr/cs-CL-0104010} and in online articles by Oleg Kiselyov using Haskell's type inference mechanism. However, the algorithm described there is basically the same as \cite{DBLP:conf/flops/KiselyovBFS08}, focusing on Peano and binary arithmetics.

nodes.name: Dedicated sparse set data structures
nodes.statement: Efficient representation of sparse sets are usually based on a dedicated data structure \cite{Briggs93anefficient} and they cannot be at the same time used for arithmetic computations as it is the case with our tree-based encoding.

nodes.name: Integer decision diagrams
nodes.statement: In \cite{vu09} integer decision diagrams are introduced providing a compressed representation for sparse integers, sets and various other data types. However likewise \cite{sac12} and \cite{ppdp10tarau}, and by contrast to those proposed in this paper, they do not compress dense sets or numbers.
nodes.statement_short: Integer decision diagrams compress sparse integers and sets but, unlike the tree representation, not dense ones.

nodes.name: Ranking and unranking functions
nodes.statement: {\em Ranking} functions (bijections between data types and natural numbers) can be traced back to G\"{o}del numberings \cite{Goedel:31} associated to formulae. Together with their inverse {\em unranking} functions they are also used in combinatorial generation algorithms \cite{conf/mfcs/MartinezM03,knuth06draft}.

nodes.name: Connecting heterogeneous data types through bijections
nodes.statement: As a fresh look at the topic, we mention recent work in the context of functional programming on connecting heterogeneous data types through bijective mappings and natural number encodings \cite{everybit,complambda,calc10tarau}.

nodes.name: Average performance comparable to the binary data type B
nodes.statement: We have seen that the average performance of arithmetic computations with trees of type {\tt T} is comparable, up to small constant factors, to computations performed with the binary data type {\tt B} and it outperforms them by an arbitrarily large margin on the interesting special cases favoring the tree representations.
nodes.statement_short: Tree arithmetic matches binary arithmetic up to constants on average and wins by an arbitrarily large margin in special cases.
assumptions: arithmetic computations with trees of type {\tt T}
conclusions: comparable, up to small constant factors, to computations performed with the binary data type {\tt B}
it outperforms them by an arbitrarily large margin on the interesting special cases favoring the tree representations

nodes.name: Are binary trees a basis for a practical arbitrary integers package?
nodes.statement: Still, does that mean that such binary trees can be used as a basis for a practical arbitrary integers package?

nodes.name: Planned hybrid of machine words and trees
nodes.statement: Native arbitrary length integer libraries like GMP or BigInteger take advantage of fast arithmetic on 64 bit words. To match their performance, we plan to switch between bitstring representations for numbers fitting in a machine word and a a tree representation for numbers not fitting in a machine word.
nodes.statement_short: Future work: switch between machine-word bitstrings and trees depending on the magnitude of the number.

nodes.name: Common feature of the compactly represented number families
nodes.statement: We have shown that some interesting number-theoretical entities like Mersenne, Fermat and perfect numbers have significantly more compact representations with our tree-based numbers. One may observe their common feature: they are all represented in terms of exponents of 2, successor/predecessor and specialized multiplication operations.
nodes.statement_short: Mersenne, Fermat and perfect numbers compress well because all are built from exponents of 2, successor/predecessor and specialized multiplication.
assumptions: some interesting number-theoretical entities like Mersenne, Fermat and perfect numbers
conclusions: have significantly more compact representations with our tree-based numbers
they are all represented in terms of exponents of 2, successor/predecessor and specialized multiplication operations

nodes.name: The fundamental theoretical challenge
nodes.statement: The fundamental theoretical challenge raised at this point is the following: {\em can other number-theoretically interesting operations, with possible applications to cryptography be also expressed succinctly in terms of our tree-based data type? Is it possible to reduce the complexity of some other important operations, besides those found so far?}
nodes.statement_short: Which further number-theoretic operations (e.g. for cryptography) admit succinct tree expressions and lower complexity?

nodes.name: Methodology for finding succinct representations
nodes.statement: The methodology to be used relies on two key components, that have been proven successful so far, in discovering succinct representations for Mersenne, Fermat and perfect numbers, as well as low complexity algorithms for operations like {\tt bitsize} and {\tt exp2}: \begin{itemize} \item partial evaluation of functional programs with respect to known data types and operations on them, as well as the use of other program transformations \item salient number-theoretical observations, provable by induction, that relate operations on our tree data types to known identities and number-theoretical algorithms \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: Two tools: partial evaluation/program transformation, and number-theoretic observations provable by induction.

nodes.name: primes (generic prime number generator)
nodes.statement:
class SpecialComputations n => Benchmarks n where
  primes :: [n]

  primes = s (s e) : filter is_prime (odds_from (s (s (s e)))) where
    odds_from x = x : odds_from (s (s x))

    is_prime p = [p]==to_primes p

    to_primes n = to_factors n p ps where
       (p:ps) = primes

    to_factors n p ps | cmp (mul p p) n == GT = [n]
    to_factors n p ps | e_ r =  p : to_factors q p ps where
       (q,r) = div_and_rem n p
    to_factors n p (hd:tl) = to_factors n hd tl
nodes.statement_short: Lazy trial-division prime generator: a number is prime when its factorization is itself.

nodes.name: Lucas-Lehmer primality test
nodes.statement:
lucas_lehmer :: n -> Bool
  lucas_lehmer p = e_ y where
    p_2 = s' (s' p)
    four = i (o e)
    m  = exp2 p
    m' = s' m
    y = f p_2 four

    f k n | e_ k = n
    f k n = r where 
      x = f (s' k) n
      y = s' (s' (mul x x))
      --r = reminder y m'
      r = fastmod y m 

    -- fast computation of k mod 2^p-1  
    fastmod k m | k == s' m = e
    fastmod k m | LT == cmp k m = k
    fastmod k m = fastmod (add q r) m where
       (q,r) = div_and_rem k m

  -- exponents leading to Mersenne primes
  mersenne_prime_exps :: [n]
  mersenne_prime_exps = filter lucas_lehmer primes

  -- actual Mersenne primes
  mersenne_primes :: [n]
  mersenne_primes = map f mersenne_prime_exps where
    f p = s' (exp2 p)
nodes.statement_short: Lucas-Lehmer test: iterate $x \mapsto x^2-2$ modulo $2^p-1$ using a fast mod, then filter the primes to get Mersenne prime exponents.
nodes.origin_citation: Lucas-Lehmer primality test for Mersenne numbers

nodes.name: Ackerman function
nodes.statement:
ack :: n->n->n
  ack x n | e_ x = s n
  ack m1 x | e_ x = ack (s' m1) (s e)
  ack m1 n1 = ack (s' m1) (ack m1 (s' n1))
nodes.statement_short: The Ackermann function, used as a stress test for successor and predecessor.

nodes.name: Collatz conjecture equivalent to termination of nsyr
nodes.statement: It is easy to show that the Collatz conjecture is true iff the function {\tt nsyr}, implementing the n-th iterate of the {\em Syracuse function}, always terminates:
assumptions: the function {\tt nsyr}, implementing the n-th iterate of the {\em Syracuse function}
conclusions: the Collatz conjecture is true iff the function {\tt nsyr} ... always terminates

nodes.name: syracuse and nsyr
nodes.statement:
syracuse  :: n->n
  -- n->c'' (3n+2)
  syracuse n = c'' (add n (i n))

  nsyr :: n->[n]
  nsyr n | e_ n = [e]
  nsyr n = n : nsyr (syracuse n)
nodes.statement_short: The Syracuse function expressed as $n \mapsto c''(3n+2)$, iterated by {\tt nsyr} until it reaches 0.

nodes.name: benchmark (CPU time measurement)
nodes.statement:
benchmark mes f = do
  x<-getCPUTime
  print f
  y<-getCPUTime
  let time=(y-x) `div` 1000000000
  return (mes++" :time="++(show time))
nodes.statement_short: Measure the CPU time of evaluating a no-argument top level function and report it in milliseconds.
input: a no argument toplevel function {\tt f} received as a parameter

nodes.name: Benchmark suite bm1t..bm8n
nodes.statement:
bm1t = benchmark "ack 3 7 on t" (ack (t (toInteger 3)) (t (toInteger 7)))
bm1b = benchmark "ack 3 7 on b" (ack (b (toInteger 3)) (b (toInteger 7)))
bm1n = benchmark "ack 3 7 on n" (ack (n (toInteger 3)) (n (toInteger 7)))

bm2t = benchmark "exp2 t" (exp2 (exp2 (t (toInteger 14))))
bm2b = benchmark "exp2 b" (exp2 (exp2 (b (toInteger 14))))
bm2n = benchmark "exp2 n" (exp2 (exp2 (n (toInteger 14))))

bm3 tvar = benchmark "sparse_set on a type" (n (bitsize (from_set ps)))
  where ps = map tvar [101,2002..100000]

bm4t =benchmark "bitsize of Mersenne 45"  (n (bitsize mersenne45))
bm5t = benchmark "bitsize of Perfect 45" (n (bitsize perfect45))

bm6t = benchmark "large leftshift" (leftshift n n) where
  n = t prime45

bm3' tvar m = benchmark "to/from list on a type" 
              (n (bitsize (from_list (to_list (from_list ps)))))
  where ps = map tvar [101,2002..3000+m]

bm3'' tvar m = benchmark "to/from list on a type" 
              (n (bitsize (from_list (to_list (from_list ps)))))
  where ps = map (dual.tvar) [101,2002..3000+m]

bm7t = benchmark "primes on t" 
  (last (take 100 ps)) where ps = primes :: [T]
bm7b = benchmark "primes on b" 
  (last (take 100 ps)) where ps = primes :: [B]
bm7n = benchmark "primes on n" 
  (last (take 100 ps)) where ps = primes :: [Integer]

bm8t = benchmark "mersenne on t" 
  (last (take 7 ps)) where ps = mersenne_primes :: [T]
bm8b = benchmark "mersenne on b" 
  (last (take 7 ps)) where ps = mersenne_primes :: [B]
bm8n = benchmark "mersenne on n" 
  (last (take 7 ps)) where ps = mersenne_primes :: [Integer]
nodes.statement_short: The benchmark definitions behind the timing table: Ackermann, iterated exp2, sparse set encoding, bitsize of giant numbers, large leftshift, prime generation and Mersenne prime tests, each on the three instances.

nodes.name: Syracuse/Collatz test and compression benchmarks
nodes.statement:
test_syr tvar m = maximum (map length (map (nsyr . tvar) [0..m]))

compress_syr tvar m = r where
  nss = map (nsyr . tvar) [0..m]
  r = maximum (map (n.bitsize) (map from_list nss))

-- overflows for m>2 except for tvar=t
compress_syr_twice tvar m = r  where
  nss = map (nsyr . tvar) [0..m]
  r = (n.bitsize) (from_list (map from_list nss))

bm9 tvar = benchmark "test syracuse" (test_syr tvar 2000)

bm10 tvar = benchmark "compress syracuse" (compress_syr tvar 100)

bm11 tvar = benchmark "compress syracuse_twice" r where
            r = compress_syr_twice tvar 20
nodes.statement_short: Tests the Syracuse iteration up to {\tt m} and measures the bitsize of the list-encoded orbits, once and twice compressed.

nodes.name: tsize (size of a tree-represented natural number)
nodes.statement:
tsize T = 1
tsize (V x xs) = 1+ sum (map tsize (x:xs))
tsize (W x xs) = 1+ sum (map tsize (x:xs))
nodes.statement_short: Count the nodes of a tree-represented natural number recursively.

nodes.name: kth (k-th iteration of a function application)
nodes.statement:
kth _ k x | e_ k  = x
kth f k x  = f (kth f (s' k) x)
nodes.statement_short: Apply {\tt f} exactly {\tt k} times.

nodes.name: Assertions relating iterated o/i applications to powers of 2
nodes.statement:
-- relation between iterations of o,i and power of 2 
a1 k = pow (i e) k == s (kth o k e) 
a2 k = pow (i e) k == s (s (kth i (s'  k) e))

-- relations between power operations and multiplication
a3 n b = (u==v,u,v) where
 m = pow (i e) n
 u = kth o n b
 v = s' (mul m (s b))
 
a4 x y = (a==b,a,b) where 
  a = mul (pow (i e) x) y
  b = s (kth o x (s' y))
nodes.statement_short: Testable identities: $2^k$ equals the successor of $k$ iterated {\tt o} applications, and multiplying by $2^x$ equals $x$ iterated {\tt o} applications up to successor/predecessor.
conclusions: a1 k = pow (i e) k == s (kth o k e)
a2 k = pow (i e) k == s (s (kth i (s'  k) e))
a4 x y = (a==b,a,b) where a = mul (pow (i e) x) y b = s (kth o x (s' y))
